correctness.rationale: On \(\alpha+\beta=2\), the exact total-population equation is \(\dot N=N(1-N)\). Stationarity of \(\log N\) and \(N\) gives \(\mathbb E[N]=\mathbb E[N^2]=1\), hence \(N=1\) almost surely. Logarithmic antiderivative tests in each species give the conditional weighted-competition load; combining that law with \(N=1\) and \(\alpha\ne1\) yields equal conditional means of the two competitors on every abundance fiber. The per-capita growth identities are then pointwise, and the exact variance formula follows from the pairwise-difference identity and the proved means \(1/3\). The packaged checker verifies every polynomial and rational reduction.

originality.rationale: The invariant plane \(x+y+z=1\), the neutral \(\alpha+\beta=2\) periodic regime, integrability questions, and global mean-value literature were treated as prior coverage and excluded from the novelty claim. The surviving statement is stronger and distribution-level: after conditioning on any one species abundance, the other two species have exactly equal conditional means, with the explicit value half of the remaining total population. The resulting exact relation between summed squared per-capita speeds and the total abundance variance is likewise not implied by known global mean or orbit-existence statements. Direct semantic searches over conditional, fiberwise, per-capita-variance, and neutral-simplex formulations found no same-object implication.

value.rationale: The neutral May–Leonard family is a canonical model of cyclic three-species competition, and its classical geometry is organized by the invariant population simplex. The accepted theorem gives that geometry a distribution-level statistical meaning: after fixing the abundance of any one species, the other two competitors have exactly equal conditional mean abundance even though their cyclic interaction coefficients are unequal. The resulting fluctuation identity ties total squared per-capita growth directly to cross-species abundance heterogeneity with the exact coefficient \(3(\alpha-1)^2\). This supplies a self-contained diagnostic for periodic-orbit or stationary data on the neutral simplex and is stronger than previously known global means without requiring a new orbit-existence theorem.
